Atlas is a small search engine that learns to read.

The project began as a question about text. What does it mean for a machine
to understand a document? The honest answer is that no machine understands a
document the way a person does. A person reads the words and builds a picture
in the mind. A machine sees numbers. The art of search is the art of choosing
the right numbers so that documents about similar things get similar numbers.

A tokenizer is the first door. Every text must pass through it. The tokenizer
cuts a string into pieces called tokens, and every token has a number. That is
all a model ever sees: numbers. If the tokenizer is careless, the model is
built on sand. If the tokenizer is careful, the model has a fair chance.

Byte pair encoding is the classic way to build a tokenizer. You start with the
smallest pieces there are, the 256 possible bytes. Then you read a corpus and
count which two pieces sit next to each other most often. You merge that pair
into one new piece, and you repeat. After enough merges, common words like the,
and, and said become single tokens, while rare words stay as several pieces.
The result is a vocabulary that bends toward the language it was trained on.

The training loop is simple to describe and easy to get wrong. First, split the
corpus into words with a pattern. Second, count every pair of adjacent pieces
across all the words, weighted by how often each word appears. Third, find the
pair with the highest count and merge it everywhere it occurs. Fourth, add the
merged piece to the vocabulary and give it the next free rank. Then go back to
the second step and keep going until the vocabulary is large enough. The rank
of a merged piece matters later, because encoding replays the merges in rank
order. A low rank means the merge happened early, which means the pieces were
common, which means the merge should win over later merges during encoding.

Encoding is the twin of training. To encode a new string, split it the same
way, then look at every adjacent pair of pieces and find the pair whose merge
has the lowest rank. Merge that pair, look again, and keep going until no pair
left in the string has a recorded merge. The lowest rank wins because the
earliest merges in training were the most frequent ones. When you replay the
merges in that order, a trained tokenizer and a fresh encoding agree with each
other. This agreement is the whole trick. A tokenizer is nothing more than a
table of ranks plus a rule about always taking the lowest rank first.

Splitting the text into words before merging is called pre-tokenization. The
pattern decides where merges may never cross. Without it, a merge might glue
the end of one word to the start of the next, and the vocabulary would fill up
with junk that never helps. Most patterns keep letters together, keep digits in
small groups, keep punctuation apart, and treat runs of spaces with care. The
care with spaces matters more than it sounds. A space before a word often
carries meaning about where one word ends and the next begins, and models that
read code care about every single space. Whitespace at the end of a line is
different from whitespace in the middle of a sentence, and the pattern says so.

Why bytes and not letters? Bytes are honest. A string is bytes in the end, and
if the tokenizer works on bytes, then any input at all can be encoded and
decoded without loss. There is no unknown character, no token for failure, no
empty answer. Emoji, accents, scripts from every language, all of them are just
bytes, and the vocabulary grows to cover the byte patterns that the corpus
shows most often. Rare scripts cost more tokens than common ones, which is a
real fairness problem, but it is a problem you can measure.

A search engine built on tokens has a long road ahead of it. After the
tokenizer comes the embedder, which turns a token sequence into a vector. The
vector lives in a space where distance means something like meaning. Two
chunks of text about the same topic land near each other. A question lands
near its answers. Nobody writes down where things land. The model learns the
space from data, and the space is the model.

Vectors alone are not search. Search needs an index. The simplest index is no
index at all: store every vector and compare a query against every single one.
This brute force scan is slow in the large and honest in the small. It is the
right first index because it gives exact answers. Every later index, however
clever, must be measured against the brute force truth. Recall is the name of
that measurement. If an index returns the top ten results and only eight of
them match the true top ten, the recall at ten is zero point eight.

Faster indexes trade exactness for speed. A graph index builds a lattice of
neighbors and walks it greedily, hoping the walk finds the true nearest
neighbors most of the time. Quantization packs each vector into fewer bytes
and accepts some error in the comparison. Clustering splits the space into
cells and only searches the promising ones. Every one of these tricks adds a
knob, a failure mode, and a benchmark to run. The honest engineer measures
recall and latency together and reports both, because either one alone is a
half truth.

Chunking sits between documents and vectors. A long document makes a weak
single vector, because a vector that must stand for everything stands for
nothing. So documents are cut into chunks, and each chunk is embedded on its
own. Cut too fine and every chunk loses context. Cut too coarse and the
vector blurs. The size of a chunk is measured in tokens, not characters,
because the embedder counts tokens. This is why the tokenizer is the first
door: even chunking leans on it.

Evaluation closes the loop. You write queries, you mark which chunks are the
known good answers, and you measure how often the system returns them at the
top. The same queries must run against every embedder and every index and
every retrieval mode, or the numbers are not comparable. A small evaluation
set run honestly beats a large one run sloppily. When the hybrid retrieval
arrives, graph walks over entity relations, vector scan over chunk
embeddings, the same questions get asked again: what recall, at what cost,
on which queries.

The graph half of Atlas comes later. Entities are pulled from text, edges
connect entities that mention, cite, or resemble each other, and a walk over
that graph can pull in context that no embedding would rank highly. Vector
search finds what sounds alike. Graph search finds what is connected. Neither
one wins everywhere, and the plan is to measure rather than guess.

Rust is a good language for all of this. The borrow checker makes the heap
and the vector and the graph explicit, which is exactly the kind of detail a
learning project wants on the table. Writing a priority queue merge by hand
teaches more than any chapter, because the compiler refuses to let the bugs
stay invisible. The plan is to write the naive merge first, then the heap
driven merge, then measure them, and let the numbers end the argument.

Small tools, measured steps, honest numbers. That is the whole method. A
tokenizer that matches a reference. An index that beats the brute force scan
without losing recall. A graph that pulls in neighbors the vectors missed.
Every claim checked against a benchmark, every benchmark committed, every
number reported even when it is ugly. That is how a learning project earns
the right to be called a search engine.

The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog while the calm cat watches the
rain from the warm window. Pack my box with five dozen liquor jugs. How
vexingly quick daft zebras jump. Sphinx of black quartz, judge my vow. The
five boxing wizards jump quickly and the job requires extra pluck and skill.

She sells sea shells by the sea shore, and the shells she sells are surely
from the south sea. Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers. A peck of
pickled peppers Peter Piper picked. If Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled
peppers, where is the peck of pickled peppers Peter Piper picked?

To be, or not to be, that is the question. Whether it is nobler in the mind
to suffer the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, or to take arms
against a sea of troubles, and by opposing end them. All the world is a
stage, and all the men and women merely players. They have their exits and
their entrances, and one man in his time plays many parts.

It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of
wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief, it was
the epoch of incredulity, it was the season of light, it was the season of
darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair.

In the beginning the Universe was created. This has made a lot of people
very angry and been widely regarded as a bad move. The ships hung in the
sky in much the same way that bricks do not. Time is an illusion. Lunchtime
doubly so. The answer to the great question of life, the universe and
everything is forty two.

The engine room hums while the index grows. One hundred thousand vectors
float in a contiguous block of memory, each one normalized so that a dot
product is a cosine. The query vector lands, the scan begins, and in a few
milliseconds the top ten chunks float to the top with their scores. It is
not clever. It is correct. Cleverness comes later, and only if it pays rent.

Later the graph wakes up. Nodes for people, places, projects, and papers.
Edges that say mentions, cites, and resembles. A personal page rank walk
starts from the seed chunks and drifts along the edges, and the drift pulls
in a project that never once used the words in the query but is exactly what
the query was for. Hybrid retrieval is a vector scan and a graph walk
shaking hands, and the evaluation harness keeps the score.
